specStatements.text: There are two ways of joining electrical components, in series and in parallel. Some circuits include both series and parallel parts.
• there is the same current through each component
• the total potential difference of the power supply is shared between the components
• the total resistance of two components is the sum of the resistance of each component.
• the potential difference across each component is the same
• the total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components
• the total resistance of two resistors is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.
• use circuit diagrams to construct and check series and parallel circuits that include a variety of common circuit components
• describe the difference between series and parallel circuits
• explain qualitatively why adding resistors in series increases the total resistance whilst adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance
• explain the design and use of dc series circuits for measurement and testing purposes
• calculate the currents, potential differences and resistances in dc series circuits
• solve problems for circuits which include resistors in series using the concept of equivalent resistance.
Students are not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No reciprocal formula (1/R_total = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2) or product-over-sum shortcut appears anywhere in this content, and no item asks a student to work out a numerical value for the combined resistance of a parallel pair. Parallel resistance is treated only as the qualitative statement the specification does require: the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor, explained qualitatively by the extra path for charge. Where a numerical value is used at all (q19) the student is asked which value is possible, a judgement that is made from the 'less than the smallest' rule alone and needs no parallel calculation. All calculation items (q02, q04, q12, q13, q15, q18) are confined to dc series circuits, as required by the specification.

concepts.term: Series connection
concepts.definition: Components are connected in series when they are joined one after another in a single loop, so there is only one path for charge to follow. Every charge that passes through one component must pass through all the others.

concepts.term: Parallel connection
concepts.definition: Components are connected in parallel when each one is joined across the same two points, so each component sits on its own branch. There is more than one path for charge to follow between those two points.

concepts.term: Circuits with both series and parallel parts
concepts.definition: There are two ways of joining electrical components, in series and in parallel, and some circuits include both. For example, a single resistor joined in series with the cell may supply two further resistors that are joined in parallel with each other. Each part of such a circuit obeys the rule for the way it is joined.

concepts.term: Current in a series circuit
concepts.definition: For components connected in series there is the same current through each component. An ammeter placed anywhere in the single loop gives the same reading, because charge is not used up as it passes through a component.

concepts.term: Sharing of potential difference in series
concepts.definition: For components connected in series the total potential difference of the power supply is shared between the components. The individual potential differences add up to the supply potential difference, and the largest share is across the component with the largest resistance.

concepts.term: Total resistance in series
concepts.definition: For components connected in series the total resistance of two components is the sum of the resistance of each component. Adding a further resistor in series therefore always makes the total resistance larger.

concepts.term: R_total = R_1 + R_2
concepts.definition: The equation for two resistors joined in series, given in the specification as R_total = R_1 + R_2. It is one of the equations students are expected to recall and apply, not one that is provided.

concepts.term: Resistance and its unit
concepts.definition: Resistance is given the symbol R and is measured in ohms, symbol Ω. Every resistance quoted or calculated in this section, including a total resistance found from R_total = R_1 + R_2, is written with the unit Ω.

concepts.term: Potential difference in a parallel circuit
concepts.definition: For components connected in parallel the potential difference across each component is the same. Each branch is joined across the same two points, so each branch has the full supply potential difference across it.

concepts.term: Total current in a parallel circuit
concepts.definition: For components connected in parallel the total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components. The current from the supply divides between the branches and recombines, so the branch currents add up to the total.

concepts.term: Total resistance of two resistors in parallel
concepts.definition: For two resistors connected in parallel the total resistance is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor. A numerical calculation of this total resistance is not required.

concepts.term: Circuit diagram
concepts.definition: A drawing that uses standard circuit symbols and straight connecting lines to show how components are joined. Circuit diagrams are used to construct series and parallel circuits containing a variety of common components, and to check that a circuit that has been built matches the intended one.

concepts.term: Connecting an ammeter
concepts.definition: An ammeter measures current and is always connected in series with the component whose current is being measured, so that the same current passes through the meter and the component.

concepts.term: Connecting a voltmeter
concepts.definition: A voltmeter measures potential difference and is always connected in parallel across the component, so that the meter and the component have the same potential difference across them.

concepts.term: Why adding resistors in series increases total resistance
concepts.definition: In series there is a single path, so charge must pass through every resistor in turn and each one opposes its flow. The oppositions add, so the total resistance rises and, for the same supply potential difference, the current in the circuit falls.

concepts.term: Why adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance
concepts.definition: Each resistor added in parallel provides an extra path for charge, and each branch has the full supply potential difference across it. The total current drawn from the supply therefore increases, which means the total resistance of the combination has fallen below that of the smallest individual resistor.

concepts.term: Equivalent resistance
concepts.definition: The resistance of the single resistor that could replace a combination of resistors without changing the current drawn from the supply. For resistors in series the equivalent resistance is found by adding them, R_total = R_1 + R_2, which turns a multi-resistor problem into a single-resistor one.

concepts.term: dc series circuit for measurement and testing
concepts.definition: A test circuit in which the component under test, an ammeter and a variable resistor are joined in series with a dc supply, with a voltmeter connected in parallel across the component. Because the components are in series, the ammeter reads exactly the current in the component under test, and the voltmeter reads the potential difference across it alone.

concepts.term: Variable resistor in a test circuit
concepts.definition: A resistor whose resistance can be changed. Placed in series, it changes the total resistance of the circuit and so changes the current through every component in the loop, which lets a range of readings be taken from one supply without changing the supply itself.

concepts.term: Using V = I R in series calculations
concepts.definition: Calculations of the currents, potential differences and resistances in a dc series circuit use potential difference = current × resistance, V = I R (from section 4.2.1.3), applied together with the series rules: the same current through each component, the supply potential difference shared between the components, and R_total = R_1 + R_2.

concepts.term: Effect of a break in the circuit
concepts.definition: A key difference between the two ways of joining components. A series circuit has one path, so a break anywhere in it stops the current everywhere. A parallel circuit has more than one path, so a break in one branch leaves the other branches with a complete path and they keep working.

misconceptions.question: In a series circuit an ammeter is placed before a lamp and a second ammeter after it. How do the two readings compare?
misconceptions.correct: The two ammeters give the same reading, because there is the same current through each component in series.
misconceptions.misconception: The current is used up as it goes through the lamp, so the ammeter after the lamp reads less than the one before it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that the lamp 'uses' or 'consumes' electricity and transfer that to the current itself, rather than to the energy transferred by the charge.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is not used up; the same charge that enters a component leaves it. What falls across the lamp is the potential difference, not the current. In series the current is the same through every component.

misconceptions.question: Two identical lamps are in series with a cell. The cell supplies a current of 0.4 A. What is the current through each lamp?
misconceptions.correct: 0.4 A through each lamp, because in series there is the same current through each component.
misconceptions.misconception: The current is shared between the components, so each lamp gets half of it, 0.2 A.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The sharing rule for series circuits is remembered but attached to the wrong quantity: it is the potential difference that is shared, not the current.
misconceptions.correction: In series it is the total potential difference of the power supply that is shared between the components. The current is the same through each of them.

misconceptions.question: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the potential difference across each lamp?
misconceptions.correct: 12 V across each lamp, because in parallel the potential difference across each component is the same.
misconceptions.misconception: The 12 V is shared between the two branches, so each lamp has 6 V across it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The series sharing rule is applied to a parallel circuit, because 'sharing' is remembered as a general rule for circuits with more than one component.
misconceptions.correction: Sharing of potential difference applies to components in series. Components in parallel are connected across the same two points, so each has the full supply potential difference across it.

misconceptions.question: A 10 Ω resistor and a 20 Ω resistor are in parallel across a supply. How do the branch currents compare?
misconceptions.correct: The 10 Ω branch carries the larger current; the two branch currents add up to the total current in the whole circuit.
misconceptions.misconception: The current from the supply always splits equally, so each branch carries half of the total whatever its resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'The current splits' is remembered as 'the current halves', and the role of resistance in deciding each branch current is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Each branch has the same potential difference across it, so the branch with the lower resistance carries the larger current. The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components.

misconceptions.question: A second resistor is connected in parallel with the first. What happens to the total resistance of the circuit?
misconceptions.correct: The total resistance falls, and becomes less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding another resistor must add resistance, so the total resistance goes up whichever way the resistor is connected.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'resistor' is treated as something that always obstructs, so any extra one is assumed to obstruct more, without thinking about the extra path it creates.
misconceptions.correction: A resistor added in parallel creates an extra path for charge, so more current is drawn from the supply for the same potential difference. That means the total resistance has fallen. Only resistors added in series increase the total resistance.

misconceptions.question: A 4 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. What can be said about the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It is less than 4 Ω, because the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the smallest individual resistor.
misconceptions.misconception: You add them, so the total resistance is 10 Ω.
misconceptions.whyItArises: R_total = R_1 + R_2 is the only resistance equation given in this section, so it gets applied to every combination of resistors regardless of how they are joined.
misconceptions.correction: R_total = R_1 + R_2 applies only to resistors joined in series. For two resistors in parallel the total is less than the smallest of them; a numerical value is not required at GCSE.

misconceptions.question: A 4 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Is the total resistance 5 Ω?
misconceptions.correct: No. The total resistance is less than 4 Ω, the smallest of the two resistances.
misconceptions.misconception: When two resistors are combined you take the average, so the total is somewhere between the two values.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the answer is not the sum, and averaging feels like a safe compromise that keeps the answer 'between' the two given numbers.
misconceptions.correction: The total resistance of two resistors in parallel lies below both values, not between them, because the extra branch lets more current flow for the same potential difference.

misconceptions.question: Where should a voltmeter be placed to measure the potential difference across a resistor?
misconceptions.correct: In parallel, connected across the resistor.
misconceptions.misconception: The voltmeter goes in the circuit loop, in series with the resistor, so that the charge passes through it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ammeters are met first and go in the loop, so a voltmeter is assumed to be fitted the same way; students also picture a meter as something the current must pass through to register.
misconceptions.correction: Potential difference is measured between two points, so the voltmeter is connected across the component, in parallel with it. Placing it in series would break the measurement and reduce the circuit current.

misconceptions.question: Where should an ammeter be placed to measure the current through a lamp?
misconceptions.correct: In series with the lamp, in the same loop.
misconceptions.misconception: The ammeter should be connected across the lamp, in parallel, so that it does not slow the current down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Once students learn that a voltmeter goes across a component, the two meters get swapped; 'not interfering with the circuit' is also misread as staying out of the loop.
misconceptions.correction: An ammeter must carry the current it measures, so it goes in series with the component. In series there is the same current through each component, so the meter reads the current in that component.

misconceptions.question: A 2 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are in series, with the 2 Ω nearer the positive terminal. Which has the larger potential difference across it?
misconceptions.correct: The 6 Ω resistor, because the larger share of the supply potential difference is across the larger resistance.
misconceptions.misconception: The component nearest the positive terminal gets the potential difference first, so it takes the bigger share and a lamp there would be brighter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is pictured as travelling round the loop 'spending' energy as it goes, so whatever it reaches first is imagined to receive the most.
misconceptions.correction: The order of components in a series loop does not change how the potential difference is shared. The share depends on the resistances, and the current is the same at every point in the loop.

misconceptions.question: A 9 V supply is in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 7 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across each?
misconceptions.correct: 2 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 7 V across the 7 Ω resistor; the two add up to the 9 V supply.
misconceptions.misconception: The supply potential difference is shared equally between the components, so each resistor has 4.5 V across it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Shared' is read as 'shared equally', as it usually is in everyday language, and the resistances are not used at all.
misconceptions.correction: The total potential difference of the supply is shared between the components in proportion to their resistances, because the same current is in each and V = I R. Equal shares occur only when the resistances are equal.

misconceptions.question: Two resistors are in series with a 6 V battery. What is the potential difference across each resistor?
misconceptions.correct: The two potential differences are smaller than 6 V and add up to 6 V.
misconceptions.misconception: Each component in the circuit has the full 6 V of the battery across it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The parallel rule that each component has the supply potential difference across it is applied to a series circuit, or the battery is imagined to deliver its full voltage to everything it is connected to.
misconceptions.correction: Each component has the full supply potential difference across it only when the components are in parallel. In series the supply potential difference is shared between the components.

misconceptions.question: A 5 Ω resistor and a 20 Ω resistor are joined in parallel. What is the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: Less than 5 Ω; the exact value is not required at GCSE.
misconceptions.misconception: The total resistance is 5 Ω, because the current takes the easiest path and simply ignores the 20 Ω branch.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is half-remembered as 'the total is the smallest resistor' rather than 'less than the smallest resistor', helped by the idea that charge chooses one route.
misconceptions.correction: Both branches carry current, because both have the full supply potential difference across them. The extra branch adds to the total current, so the total resistance is below 5 Ω, not equal to it.

misconceptions.question: Two identical 10 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: Less than 10 Ω, because the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the smallest individual resistor.
misconceptions.misconception: The resistors are identical, so nothing changes and the total resistance is still 10 Ω.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'less than the smallest' rule is thought to apply only when the two resistances differ, so identical resistors are assumed to be a special case where the value stays put.
misconceptions.correction: The rule holds for any two resistors in parallel, identical or not. Two identical branches draw twice the current a single one would, so the total resistance is below 10 Ω.

misconceptions.question: The resistance of a variable resistor in a series test circuit is increased. What happens to the current?
misconceptions.correct: The current falls in every part of the circuit, because the total resistance of the series circuit has increased.
misconceptions.misconception: Turning the resistance up increases the current, because you are turning the component up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A variable resistor is treated like a volume control, where 'more' always means a bigger effect, and the inverse relationship between resistance and current is not applied.
misconceptions.correction: For a fixed supply potential difference, a larger total resistance gives a smaller current. Since the components are in series, that smaller current is the current through every component.

misconceptions.question: A 12 V supply is in series with a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?
misconceptions.correct: 1.0 A, found from the total resistance of 12 Ω using V = I R.
misconceptions.misconception: The current through the 4 Ω resistor is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A, and the current through the 8 Ω resistor is 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 A.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The supply potential difference is used with a single component's resistance, because students apply V = I R to one resistor at a time without first finding the total resistance or the shared potential differences.
misconceptions.correction: Use the supply potential difference only with the total resistance R_total = R_1 + R_2. That gives the one current in the series loop; each resistor's own potential difference then follows from V = I R for that resistor.

misconceptions.question: A third identical lamp is added in series to a circuit with two lamps. What happens to the brightness of the original lamps?
misconceptions.correct: They become dimmer, because the total resistance has increased so the current in the loop is smaller.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding another lamp adds more to the circuit, so all the lamps get brighter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More components' is read as 'more of everything', and the effect of the extra resistance on the current in the single series path is not considered.
misconceptions.correction: Resistors and lamps added in series increase the total resistance, so the current falls, and the supply potential difference is now shared between three components instead of two. All the lamps are dimmer.

misconceptions.question: Two lamps are connected in parallel and one of them is removed from its holder. What happens to the other lamp?
misconceptions.correct: It stays lit at the same brightness, because its own branch is still a complete path with the full supply potential difference across it.
misconceptions.misconception: The circuit is now broken, so the second lamp goes out as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The series experience of one broken lamp stopping everything is carried over, because a circuit is pictured as a single loop that must be complete all the way round.
misconceptions.correction: A parallel circuit provides more than one path. Breaking one branch leaves the other branch complete, and the potential difference across it is unchanged, so it keeps working.

misconceptions.question: In a parallel circuit, is the current the same at every point?
misconceptions.correct: No. The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components, so the main current is larger than any branch current.
misconceptions.misconception: Current is the same everywhere in any circuit, so the ammeter in the main circuit reads the same as an ammeter in a branch.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'The current is the same through each component' is learned for series circuits and then remembered as a rule about all circuits.
misconceptions.correction: The same current through each component is a rule for series connection only. In parallel the supply current divides between the branches, and the branch currents add to give the total.

misconceptions.question: One lamp is removed from a series circuit containing two lamps. What happens to the other lamp?
misconceptions.correct: It goes out, because a series circuit has only one path and that path is now broken.
misconceptions.misconception: The other lamp stays lit, because the current can still get to it round the rest of the loop.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is imagined as flowing out of the cell to each component in turn, rather than round one continuous path that has to be complete.
misconceptions.correction: In series there is a single path, so there must be an unbroken route through every component. A break anywhere stops the current everywhere in that loop.

misconceptions.question: The potential difference across a resistor is 12 V and the current through it is 4 A. A student writes the resistance as 3 V. What is wrong?
misconceptions.correct: The quantity found is a resistance, so it is 3 Ω: resistance, R, is measured in ohms, Ω.
misconceptions.misconception: The unit of an answer comes from the numbers that went into the sum, so a resistance worked out from volts and amps is written in volts or amps.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Units are treated as labels that travel with the numbers rather than as properties of the quantity being calculated, so the unit of the first value in the calculation is carried into the answer.
misconceptions.correction: Each quantity has its own unit whatever it was calculated from. Potential difference is in volts, current is in amps, and resistance, R, is in ohms, Ω.

mcqs.stem: A lamp and a resistor are connected in series with a cell. An ammeter between the cell and the lamp reads 0.30 A. A second ammeter is placed between the lamp and the resistor. What does it read?

options.text: Under 0.30 A, since some of the current is used up inside the lamp
options.rationale: Students who think current is consumed by a component expect the reading after the lamp to have dropped.

options.text: 0.30 A, since in series the current through each component is the same
options.rationale: For components connected in series there is the same current through each component, so both ammeters read 0.30 A.

options.text: 0.15 A, since the current is shared between the lamp and the resistor
options.rationale: The series sharing rule is applied to current instead of to potential difference, giving half of 0.30 A.

options.text: It depends on how the resistance of the resistor compares with the lamp
options.rationale: Resistance decides how the potential difference is shared, not whether the current differs from place to place in a series loop.

mcqs.stem: A 6 V battery is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?

options.text: 4 V
options.rationale: R_total = 2 Ω + 4 Ω = 6 Ω, so the current is 6 V ÷ 6 Ω = 1 A. Across the 4 Ω resistor, V = 1 A × 4 Ω = 4 V.

options.text: 3 V
options.rationale: The supply potential difference is split equally between the two resistors, ignoring their different resistances.

options.text: 6 V
options.rationale: Each series component is assumed to have the full supply potential difference across it.

options.text: 2 V
options.rationale: The shares are swapped: 2 V is the potential difference across the 2 Ω resistor, not the 4 Ω one.

mcqs.stem: A 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which statement about the total resistance of the pair is correct?

options.text: It is less than 3 Ω, below the smaller of the two resistances
options.rationale: For two resistors in parallel the total resistance is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.

options.text: It is 9 Ω, because the two resistances are added together
options.rationale: R_total = R_1 + R_2 is applied to a parallel pair, although it holds only for resistors in series.

options.text: It is 4.5 Ω, the value halfway between the two resistances
options.rationale: Averaging feels like a safe compromise and keeps the answer between the two given values.

options.text: It is 3 Ω, because charge takes the easier of the two paths
options.rationale: The rule is half-remembered as 'equal to the smallest' and the second branch is assumed to carry nothing.

mcqs.stem: A 5 Ω resistor and a 7 Ω resistor are connected in series. What single resistance could replace them without changing the current drawn from the supply?

options.rationale: The two resistances have been multiplied rather than added.
R_total = R_1 + R_2 = 5 Ω + 7 Ω = 12 Ω, the equivalent resistance of the series pair.

options.text: 6 Ω
options.rationale: The average of the two values is taken instead of their sum.

options.text: 5 Ω
options.rationale: The 'less than the smallest' idea from parallel circuits is applied to a series pair, so the smaller value is chosen.

mcqs.stem: Which equation gives the total resistance of two resistors joined in series?

options.text: R_total = R_1 − R_2
options.rationale: A student who remembers that combining resistors can give a value below the smallest reaches for subtraction here.

options.text: R_total = R_1 × R_2
options.rationale: Multiplying is chosen by students who remember only that the two values are 'combined' somehow.

options.text: R_total = R_1 + R_2
options.rationale: This is the equation given in the specification for two components in series, and it must be recalled.

options.text: R_total = ½(R_1 + R_2)
options.rationale: The averaging idea is carried over into the equation itself.

mcqs.stem: In a dc series circuit the potential difference across one resistor is 12 V and the current through it is 4 A. What is the resistance of this resistor?

options.text: 3 V
options.rationale: The number is right but the unit of the quantity the student started from is carried into the answer.

options.text: 3 A
options.rationale: The same unit error, this time taking the unit from the current used in the division.
The values are multiplied instead of divided, a frequent slip when V = I R is rearranged.

options.text: 3 Ω
options.rationale: R = V ÷ I = 12 V ÷ 4 A = 3, and the specification gives resistance, R, in ohms, Ω.

mcqs.stem: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the potential difference across the lamps?

options.text: 6 V across each lamp
options.rationale: The series sharing rule is applied to a parallel circuit, halving the supply potential difference.

options.text: 24 V across each lamp
options.rationale: The potential differences of the two branches are added, as if a parallel pair doubled the supply.

options.text: 12 V across lamp 1 only
options.rationale: The first lamp reached is assumed to take the potential difference before the other one gets any.

options.text: 12 V across each lamp
options.rationale: For components connected in parallel the potential difference across each component is the same, and equals the supply potential difference.

mcqs.stem: Two resistors are connected in parallel. The current in one branch is 0.4 A and the current in the other branch is 0.6 A. What is the reading on an ammeter in the main circuit, between the battery and the branches?

options.rationale: The series rule is applied to a parallel circuit, so the main current is assumed to match a branch current.
The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components: 0.4 A + 0.6 A.
The branch currents are assumed to be equal shares, so their average is taken as the total.
The branch currents are subtracted, as if the branches opposed each other rather than adding.

mcqs.stem: A student wants to measure both the current through a resistor and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?

options.text: Ammeter in series with the resistor, voltmeter across it
options.rationale: An ammeter must carry the current it measures, so it goes in the loop; a voltmeter measures between two points, so it goes across the component.

options.text: Ammeter across the resistor, voltmeter in series with it
options.rationale: The two meters are swapped, a very common error once students learn that one of them goes 'across'.

options.text: Both meters connected in series with the resistor
options.rationale: The voltmeter is treated like an ammeter, on the assumption that charge must pass through a meter for it to read.

options.text: Both meters connected in parallel with the resistor
options.rationale: The ammeter is kept out of the loop so that it 'does not slow the current down', which would leave it reading the wrong current.

mcqs.stem: Explain why adding a second resistor in series with the first increases the total resistance of the circuit.

options.text: The extra resistor creates a second path, so the charge is held back more strongly
options.rationale: An extra path is described, but that is what happens in parallel, and it lowers rather than raises the total resistance.

options.text: The first resistor uses up some of the current, leaving less to push round the loop
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think current is consumed as it passes through components.

options.text: There is one path, so charge passes through both resistors and the opposition adds
options.rationale: In series the single path runs through every resistor in turn, so the resistances add and the current falls for the same supply potential difference.

options.text: Adding any component to a circuit always increases its total resistance
options.rationale: A blanket rule that ignores how the component is joined, which fails for parallel connection.

mcqs.stem: Explain why adding a second resistor in parallel with the first decreases the total resistance of the circuit.

options.text: The two resistors share the current, so each of them has less work to do than before
options.rationale: Sharing is described, but sharing on its own does not explain why the total current from the supply rises.

options.text: Adding a resistor must add resistance, so the total is larger than either of them
options.rationale: Any extra resistor is assumed to obstruct more, with no account taken of the extra path.

options.text: The extra branch is another path for charge, so more current is drawn from the supply
options.rationale: Each branch has the full supply potential difference across it, so a second branch increases the total current, which means the total resistance has fallen.

options.text: The total is the average of the two resistances, so it lies between the two values
options.rationale: Averaging is used as a compromise, but the true total lies below both values.

mcqs.stem: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?

options.rationale: The full supply potential difference is divided by one resistor alone: 12 V ÷ 4 Ω.
The same error using the other resistor: 12 V ÷ 8 Ω.
R_total = 4 Ω + 8 Ω = 12 Ω, so I = V ÷ R = 12 V ÷ 12 Ω = 1.0 A.
The correct current is halved on the assumption that it is shared between the two resistors.

mcqs.stem: A 6 Ω resistor and a 9 Ω resistor are connected in series with a 30 V supply. Using the equivalent resistance of the pair, what is the current in the circuit?

options.rationale: The equivalent resistance is R_total = 6 Ω + 9 Ω = 15 Ω, so I = V ÷ R = 30 V ÷ 15 Ω = 2.0 A.
The full supply potential difference is divided by one resistor alone: 30 V ÷ 6 Ω.
The two resistances are averaged to 7.5 Ω before dividing, instead of being added.
The same one-resistor-at-a-time error using the other value: 30 V ÷ 9 Ω.

mcqs.stem: A resistor is tested using a dc circuit in which the resistor, an ammeter and a variable resistor are joined in series, with a voltmeter across the resistor. Why is this a good design for the test?

options.text: The variable resistor alters the potential difference of the supply, so several values can be tested
options.rationale: A variable resistor is imagined to control the supply directly rather than the total resistance of the loop.

options.text: The ammeter reads the current in the resistor itself, and the variable resistor changes it
options.rationale: In series there is the same current through each component, so the ammeter reading is the current in the resistor under test, while the variable resistor alters the total resistance to give a range of readings.

options.text: The ammeter is kept in parallel, so it does not change the current in the resistor under test
options.rationale: Meter placement is confused, and the stated arrangement is contradicted.

options.text: The series connection puts the full potential difference of the supply across the fixed resistor
options.rationale: The parallel rule for potential difference is applied to a series circuit.

mcqs.stem: In the series test circuit above, the resistance of the variable resistor is increased. What happens to the current through the component under test?

options.text: It rises, because a larger resistance gives the charges a bigger push round
options.rationale: The variable resistor is treated as a control that increases the effect when turned up.

options.text: It falls, because the total resistance of the series circuit is now larger
options.rationale: R_total has increased, so for the same supply potential difference the current in the single loop is smaller.

options.text: It is unchanged, because the current in a series circuit is always the same
options.rationale: 'Same current through each component' is misread as 'the current can never change'.

options.text: Only the current in the variable resistor falls, and the rest is unaffected
options.rationale: Components in series are treated as having their own separate currents.

mcqs.stem: Two lamps are lit by one battery. One lamp is unscrewed from its holder and the other stays lit at the same brightness. What does this show?

options.text: They are in series: the current simply carries on round the rest of the single loop
options.rationale: Students who do not picture the loop as continuous think a series circuit survives a break.

options.text: They are in parallel, so the remaining lamp now takes the share of the one removed
options.rationale: If potential difference were shared between branches, removing one would give the other more, so it would brighten.

options.text: They are in parallel: the remaining lamp still has a complete path and the same potential difference
options.rationale: A parallel circuit has more than one path, and each branch has the supply potential difference across it, so removing one branch leaves the other unchanged.

options.text: They are in parallel, so the current drawn from the battery is exactly the same
options.rationale: The total current is the sum of the branch currents, so removing a branch reduces it.

mcqs.stem: A circuit diagram shows a cell, a switch and two identical lamps drawn one after another in a single loop. Which statement is correct when the switch is closed?

options.text: Both light, but the lamp nearer the positive terminal is brighter
options.rationale: Position in the loop is wrongly thought to decide the share of potential difference.

options.text: Both light, with the full potential difference of the cell across each
options.rationale: The parallel rule for potential difference is applied to a series loop.

options.text: Both light, and the current divides equally between the two lamps
options.rationale: Sharing is attached to current rather than to potential difference.

options.text: Both lamps light, with the same current through each of them
options.rationale: The lamps are in series, and for components connected in series there is the same current through each component.

mcqs.stem: A 9 V supply is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 7 Ω resistor. Which statement about the potential differences is correct?

options.text: 4.5 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 4.5 V across the 7 Ω resistor
options.rationale: 'Shared' is read as 'shared equally', so the resistances are never used.

options.text: 9 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 9 V across the 7 Ω resistor
options.rationale: Every component is assumed to have the full supply potential difference across it.

options.text: 7 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 2 V across the 7 Ω resistor
options.rationale: The shares are correct in size but attached to the wrong resistors, giving the larger share to the smaller resistance.

options.text: 2 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 7 V across the 7 Ω resistor
options.rationale: The current is 9 V ÷ 9 Ω = 1 A, so V = 1 A × 2 Ω = 2 V and V = 1 A × 7 Ω = 7 V, and these add to the 9 V supply.

mcqs.stem: A 4 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which of these values could be the total resistance of the pair?

options.rationale: The two resistances are added, as they would be in series.

options.text: 8 Ω
options.rationale: The average of the two values is taken, placing the answer between them.

options.text: 4 Ω
options.rationale: The rule is misremembered as 'equal to the smallest resistor' rather than 'less than' it.

options.text: 3 Ω
options.rationale: The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor, so it must be below 4 Ω. Only this value is.

mcqs.stem: A resistor is connected in series with a battery, and this resistor supplies two further resistors that are connected in parallel with each other. Which statement about this circuit is correct?

options.text: The current in the series resistor equals the sum of the two branch currents
options.rationale: The series resistor carries the whole circuit current, and the total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components in parallel.

options.text: The current in the series resistor equals the current in each of the branches
options.rationale: The series rule is applied to the parallel part, so every current is assumed to be equal.

options.text: The potential difference of the battery is shared equally by all three resistors
options.rationale: Equal sharing is assumed, and the parallel part is treated as though it were series.

options.text: The potential difference across the series resistor is the same as the supply
options.rationale: The whole supply potential difference is given to one series component, leaving none for the parallel section.
